#### ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

```{r}
outlets <- read_csv("outlets.csv")   # load dataset

# regression task - profit (y) vs population (x)
```


```{r}
library(GGally)

ggpairs(data = outlets)    # correlation plot/matrix

# exploratory graphs
# a linear model is a good starting point
# purpose - learn about gradient descent

```



#### ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Data Splitting

```{r}
set.seed(208)
# fixes the randomness - we are all going to get the same result

library(rsample)

data_split <- initial_split(data = outlets, prop = 0.8)

# ?initial_split
# prop decides how much goes into each set - 80% training, 20% test - this is decided randomly

outlets_train <- training(data_split)   # training set
# datast we use to train our model - find b0 and b1 using gradient descent

outlets_test <- testing(data_split)   # test set

```



#### ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Implement Gradient Descent

```{r}
# define variables
# to sepcify a particular variable/column in R, use dataset$variable

x <- outlets_train$population   # input/predictor
y <- outlets_train$profit       # response

```


```{r}
# define necessary functions

# calculates y-hats given x - population value, b0-intercept, b1-slope (slide 6)
predict_y <- function(x, intercept, slope)
{
  return(intercept + (slope * x) )
}


# calculates MSE (loss/cost) - slide 6
loss_mse <- function(predictions, y)
{
  residuals = predictions - y
  
  return(mean(residuals ^ 2))
}


# calculates the gradients with respect to b0 and b1 (slide 12)
gradient <- function(x, y, predictions)
{
  residuals = predictions - y
  db0 = 2 * mean(residuals)
  db1 = 2 * mean(x * residuals)
  
  return(list("db0" = db0, "db1" = db1))
}

# d - derivative , b0 and b1 -with respect to what
# db0 - derivative of MSE wrt b0


```


```{r}
# gradient descent algorithm
# specify - starting value of b0 and b1
# alpha - learning rate or setp size
# niter - number of steps of the algorithm

gradient_descent <- function(b0, b1, alpha, niter)
{
  
  # define objects to store results
  loss_values =  rep(NA, niter)
  b0_values = rep(NA, niter)
  b1_values = rep(NA, niter)
  
  
  # gradient descent algorithm
  for (epoch in 1:niter)
  {
    
    predictions = predict_y(x, b0, b1)    # obtain predictions. y-hats
    
    loss = loss_mse(predictions, y)     # calculate MSE
    
    gradients = gradient(x, y, predictions)   # obtain gradients
    db0 = gradients$db0   # gradient with respect to b0
    db1 = gradients$db1   # gradient with respect to b1
    
    # slide 13
    b0 = b0 - db0 * alpha     # update b0
    b1 = b1 - db1 * alpha     # update b1
    
    
    # store resulting values to track progress
    loss_values[epoch] = loss
    b0_values[epoch] = b0
    b1_values[epoch] = b1
    
    
    # display loss to track progress
    if (epoch %% 10 == 0){print(paste0("Epoch: ",epoch, ", Loss: ", round(loss, 5)))}
    
  }
  
  print(paste0("Intercept: ", b0_values[niter], ", and Slope: ", b1_values[niter]))
  
  results <- data.frame(epoch = 1:niter, loss = loss_values, b0 = b0_values, b1 = b1_values)

  ggplot(data = results, aes(x = epoch, y = loss)) + geom_line(color = "steelblue")
  
}


```


```{r}
# implement the algorithm
# starting values of b0=0, b1=0
# step size is 0.1
# run for 50 iterations
gradient_descent(b0 = 0, b1 = 0, alpha = 0.01, niter = 2500)

# e+23 means 10 to the power 23
# for step size of .1, MSE is increasing - 
# second try with step size = 0.01, and trial for 50 iterations
# once MSE decreases, let's increase the number of iterations
# at 500 iterations MSE is still decreasing, change to 2500
# it's not decreasing any more, stabilized
# b0 = -3.162, b1 = 1.133 - optimal values using gradient descent

# we have got the best fit line - best in the sense which minimizes the MSE - the values of b0 and b1 that gives the smallest MSE
# b0 - expected / predicted response (profit) when x = 0 (population = 0) - sometimes the b0 value doesn't make sense, not a meanigful interpretation
# b1 (slope) - when x increaes by 1 unit (population increases by 100,000), the response is predicted / expected to increase (due to b1 being positive) by 1.133 x $1,000 dollars

```


```{r}
# plot fitted line

ggplot(data = outlets_train) +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x = population, y = profit)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = -3.162, slope = 1.133, color = "blue")

# this is the line (values of b0 and b1) that minimizes the MSE
# positive slope - increasing relationship
```


```{r}
# obtain predictions 

predict_y(x = 17, intercept = -3.162, slope = 1.133)   
# one-off prediction for population = 17

predict_y(x = outlets_train$population, intercept = -3.162, slope = 1.133) # for all the training set

```


```{r}
# test set RMSE 

test_preds <- predict_y(x = outlets_test$population, intercept = -3.162, slope = 1.133)   # predicted response for the test set

test_preds

loss_mse(predictions = test_preds, y = outlets_test$profit)   # test set MSE

sqrt(loss_mse(predictions = test_preds, y = outlets_test$profit))   # test set RMSE - Root Mean Squared Error (this is the same units as the response)

2.517/mean(outlets_test$profit)

# we are off from the observed response by 2500 dollars on average
# about half of the average

# Metrics::rmse(actual = outlets_test$profit, predicted = test_preds)

```


#### ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
### Other Option to Run Linear Regression

### with R

```{r}
# using lm() function - uses matrix algebra

model_fit <- lm(profit ~ population, data = outlets_train)

model_fit

```


```{r}
# prediction

model_preds <- predict(model_fit, newdata = outlets_test)

Metrics::rmse(actual = outlets_test$profit, predicted = model_preds)

```
